headline: Mizuho: half-year profit up 30% to ¥896 billion; full-year forecast raised 14% to ¥1.6 trillion and dividend to ¥200
takeaway: Mizuho grew profit fastest among Japan’s megabanks, up 29.9% to ¥896.5 billion in the first half, and raised its full-year forecast from ¥1.4 trillion to ¥1.6 trillion. The dividend forecast rose to ¥200 from ¥145, quarterly EPS beat the consensus by 17%, and the ADRs rose 2.2%.
results: Mizuho Financial Group reported profit attributable to shareholders of ¥896.5 billion for the six months ended September 30, up 29.9%, on ordinary income of ¥4,993.1 billion, up 15.1%. Ordinary profit rose 47.3% to ¥1,252.3 billion and earnings per share were ¥368.81. The second quarter alone came to about US$0.24 per ADS against a consensus of US$0.21.

Interest income rose 8% to ¥3,127.6 billion while interest expenses rose only 5%, widening the margin; interest on loans rose 13% and fee and commission income rose 18% to ¥688.3 billion. Comprehensive income fell 69.5% to ¥257.3 billion as higher yields reduced the value of the securities portfolio.
The interim dividend was ¥100, against ¥72.50 a year earlier, and the full-year forecast is now ¥200, up from ¥145 paid last year.
mgmt: Following the first-half result, Mizuho raised its consolidated earnings estimate for the year to March 2027 by ¥200 billion, or 14.2%, to ¥1.6 trillion, an increase of 28.1% on last year, or ¥660.42 a share. The half-year profit is 56% of the new figure.
The company revised its dividend estimate at the same time, consistent with its policy of a progressive dividend linked to earnings growth.
view: Mizuho has long been the laggard of the three megabanks, with the thinnest margins and a history of IT failures that drew regulatory penalties. This report shows it is now the biggest beneficiary of normalising Japanese rates. Ordinary profit up 47% and an 18% rise in fee income point to both higher margins and a stronger investment-banking and markets business, partly the result of its purchase of US advisory firm Greenhill in 2023.

Raising the forecast by 14% at the half-way mark is unusual for a Japanese bank, where managements tend to set targets they can comfortably beat and leave revisions to the final quarter. Doing it now, together with a 38% increase in the dividend, signals confidence that the improvement is structural rather than a few good months in the markets business.

The risk is the same as for its peers: the falling comprehensive income shows how much bond-price exposure the banks carry, and any sharp rise in long-term yields would hit capital before it helps earnings. Mizuho also has less overseas diversification than MUFG. But on these numbers, the bank that was the weakest of the three is closing the profitability gap quickly, and that is usually when the valuation gap closes too.
watch: Watch whether Mizuho keeps beating its raised forecast in the second half, the trend in securities valuation losses, and any announcement of a larger share buyback in May.
